Fit Multiple Linear Segments And Their Change Points

Source: R/mcp.R
mcp.Rd

Given a model (a list of segment formulas), mcp infers the posterior distributions of the parameters of each segment as well as the change points between segments. See details or the mcp website.

Usage

mcp(
  model,
  data,
  prior = list(),
  family = gaussian(),
  par_x = NULL,
  sample = "post",
  chains = 3,
  iter = 3000,
  warmup = 1000,
  inits = NULL,
  jags_code = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  diagnostics = list(),
  quiet = getOption("mcp_quiet", FALSE),
  cores = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  adapt = lifecycle::deprecated()
)

Arguments

model

A list of formulas, one for each segment, in the format model = list(response ~ predictors, ~ cp(...) + predictors), where cp() is optional. See mcp-formula for how segments connect and the full formula syntax. Read more.

data

Table-like data in long format (data.frame, tibble, data.table, etc.) with syntactic column names. The response variable can contain missing values, which will be imputed jointly with the parameters. Read more.

prior

Named list, e.g., prior = list(cp_1 = "dunif(0, 100)", Intercept_1 = "dnorm(0, 1)"). List names are parameter names (cp_1, Intercept_1, x_2, sigma_1, etc.) and values are a distribution string (e.g., "dnorm(0, 1) T(0, )"), a fixed value (e.g., -2.1), or the name of another parameter to share its value. Weakly informative defaults are used where priors are not specified; see them with prior_summary(). See mcp-priors for the full syntax. Read more.

family

A supported family and link function:

  • gaussian(link = "identity") or gaussian(link = "log")

  • binomial() or bernoulli() with link = "logit", "probit", or "identity"

  • poisson(link = "log") or poisson(link = "identity")

  • negbinomial(link = "log", link_shape = "log")

Read more.

par_x

String. Name of the change-point variable, i.e., the data column on which change points are located. NULL (default) auto-detects it as the only continuous variable in the formulas.

sample

One of

  • "post": Sample the posterior.

  • "prior": Sample only the prior. Use prior = TRUE explicitly in plots, summaries, and other methods to select prior draws.

  • "both": Sample both prior and posterior. Plots, summaries, etc. will default to using the posterior. Use prior = TRUE to select prior draws.

  • "none" or FALSE: Do not sample. Returns an mcpfit object without draws. This is useful if you only want to check prior strings (fit$prior), the JAGS model (fit$jags_code), etc.

chains

Positive integer. Number of chains to run.

iter

Positive integer. Number of post-warmup draws from each chain. The total number of draws is iter * chains.

warmup

Positive integer. Number of initial iterations per chain which are discarded before sampling. Set higher if needed for sampler adaptation; use diagnostics to assess convergence.

inits

A named list of initial values for the parameters, e.g., list(Intercept_1 = 10), or a list of such lists with one per chain. This can be useful if a model fails to converge (read more). Names must be stochastic nodes in fit$jags_code (lines with ~). Fixed parameters and parameters that mcp samples via reparameterization (e.g., Intercept_3 is sampled as Intercept_3_end_) cannot be initialized directly. See mcp_reparam in mcp-package. Initial values for change points must be ordered. Defaults to NULL where all chains start at equispaced change points and the prior medians. User-provided inits take precedence.

jags_code

String. Pass JAGS code to mcp to use directly. This is useful if you want to tweak the code in fit$jags_code and run it within the mcp framework. R-side simulation and prediction methods continue to use the mcp-default formulas (with warning), so they may no longer match custom JAGS code. Read more about how mcp writes JAGS code.

seed

NULL or a positive integer. Seed for the JAGS random-number generators. If NULL (default), the seed is drawn from R's random-number generator, so set.seed() before mcp() also makes sampling reproducible.

diagnostics

Named list of diagnostic warning thresholds. Available elements are rhat = 1.01, ess_bulk = 400, ess_tail = 400, ar = 0.10, and ma = 0.10. An empty list uses these defaults; a partial list overrides only the supplied values. Set an element to NULL to disable that diagnostic, or use FALSE to disable all configurable diagnostic warnings. In summary.mcpfit(), NULL inherits the settings used to fit the model, while a list or FALSE overrides the diagnostic footer.

quiet

Logical. Suppress routine JAGS output and mcp sampling-status messages? Defaults to FALSE. Use options(mcp_quiet = TRUE) to change the default for the session.

cores

Deprecated and ignored. Configure parallel processing with a future plan instead, for example future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 3). With the default future plan, chains are sampled sequentially. The argument remains available for backwards compatibility.

adapt

Deprecated; use warmup instead.

Value

An mcpfit object.

Details

Here is the demo model, which ships already fitted as demo_fit (see also mcp_example("demo")):

model = list(
  response ~ 1,  # Plateau in the first segment (Intercept_1)
  ~ 0 + time,    # Joined slope (time_2) in segment 2 which starts at cp_1
  ~ 1 + time     # Disjoined slope (Intercept_3, time_3) at cp_2
)

Segment 2 continues from where the plateau left off, while segment 3 starts afresh with a new intercept. See mcp-formula for the rules of how segments connect, the full formula syntax, and the underlying model. See mcp-priors for how to specify priors. See the mcp website for worked examples of all model features.

References

  • Lindeløv, J. K. (2020). mcp: An R Package for Regression With Multiple Change Points. OSF Preprints. doi:10.31219/osf.io/fzqxv Introduces the mcp package, formula syntax, default priors, and workflow for regression with multiple change points across generalized linear and time-series models. Newer-than-2020 versions of the paper may be available at that link. Please cite the newest version.

  • Carlin, B. P., Gelfand, A. E., & Smith, A. F. (1992). Hierarchical Bayesian Analysis of Changepoint Problems. Applied Statistics, 41(2), 389–405. doi:10.2307/2347570 Introduced the Gibbs sampling approach for continuous change points in segmented regression and hierarchical models, providing the computational foundation used by BUGS and JAGS.

Author

Jonas Kristoffer Lindeløv jonas@lindeloev.dk

Examples

# \donttest{
# Define the segments using formulas. A change point is estimated between each formula.
model = list(
  response ~ 1,  # Plateau in the first segment (Intercept_1)
  ~ 0 + time,    # Joined slope (time_2) in segment 2 which starts at cp_1
  ~ 1 + time     # Disjoined slope (Intercept_3, time_3) at cp_2
)

# Fit it and sample the prior too.
# future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 3)  # Uncomment for parallel sampling
data = mcp_example_data("demo")  # Simulated data example
demo_fit = mcp(model, data = data, sample = "both", seed = 42)

# See parameter estimates
summary(demo_fit)
#> Family: gaussian
#> Links: mu = identity; sigma = identity
#> Draws: 9000 (3 chains with iter = 3000)
#> Segments:
#>   1: response ~ 1
#>   2: ~ 0 + time
#>   3: ~ 1 + time
#> 
#> Change point parameters:
#>    parameter  mean    sd lower  upper rhat ess_bulk ess_tail  sim match
#>  cp_1        31.75 1.736 28.48 35.084 1.00     3249     4358 30.0    OK
#>  cp_2        71.12 1.004 69.48 72.776 1.00     3660     6245 70.0    OK
#> 
#> Population-level parameters:
#>    parameter  mean    sd lower  upper rhat ess_bulk ess_tail  sim match
#>  Intercept_1  9.96 0.651  8.69 11.255 1.00     4919     6791 10.0    OK
#>  time_2       0.55 0.048  0.46  0.643 1.00     5176     6667  0.5    OK
#>  Intercept_3 13.95 1.370 11.31 16.678 1.00     2254     4267 15.0    OK
#>  time_3      -0.20 0.084 -0.37 -0.039 1.00     1238     2159 -0.3    OK
#>  sigma_1      3.87 0.286  3.35  4.470 1.00     5025     5407  3.5    OK

# Visual inspection of the results
plot(demo_fit)  # Visualization of model fit/predictions

plot_pars(demo_fit)  # Parameter distributions


pp_check(demo_fit)  # Prior/Posterior predictive checks


# Test a hypothesis
hypothesis(demo_fit, "cp_1 > 30")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   hypothesis     mean    sd lower upper  prob    BF
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 cp_1 - 30 > 0  1.75  1.74 -1.52  5.08 0.836  5.13

# Make predictions
head(fitted(demo_fit))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   response  time .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    12.2   76.3  12.9 1.01   10.9    14.9
#> 2     6.35  83.5  11.4 0.714  10.0    12.8
#> 3    28.0   60.2  25.5 0.897  23.7    27.2
#> 4    15.7   74.7  13.2 1.11   11.1    15.4
#> 5    16.2   85.9  10.9 0.708   9.54   12.3
#> 6    22.3   40.1  14.5 0.649  13.1    15.6
head(predict(demo_fit))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   response  time .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    12.2   76.3  12.9  3.97   5.01   20.8
#> 2     6.35  83.5  11.4  3.94   3.67   19.2
#> 3    28.0   60.2  25.4  3.96  17.6    33.3
#> 4    15.7   74.7  13.3  3.97   5.29   21.1
#> 5    16.2   85.9  10.9  3.96   3.18   18.7
#> 6    22.3   40.1  14.5  4.01   6.73   22.2
head(predict(demo_fit, newdata = data.frame(time = c(55.545, 80, 132))))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>    time .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1  55.5 23.0   3.94  15.2    30.7
#> 2  80   12.2   3.98   4.35   19.9
#> 3 132    1.44  5.59  -9.52   12.4

# Compare to a one-intercept-only model (no change points) with default prior
model_null = list(response ~ 1)
fit_null = mcp(model_null, data = data, par_x = "time")  # fit another model here
demo_loo = loo(demo_fit)
null_loo = loo(fit_null)
loo_compare(demo_loo, null_loo)
#>   model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff diag_elpd
#>  model1       0.0     0.0      NA                    
#>  model2     -58.1     9.1    1.00                    

# Inspect the prior. Useful for prior predictive checks.
summary(demo_fit, prior = TRUE)
#> Family: gaussian
#> Links: mu = identity; sigma = identity
#> Draws: 9000 (3 chains with iter = 3000)
#> Segments:
#>   1: response ~ 1
#>   2: ~ 0 + time
#>   3: ~ 1 + time
#> 
#> Change point parameters:
#>    parameter    mean    sd  lower upper rhat ess_bulk ess_tail  sim match
#>  cp_1        34.0031 23.49   1.81  84.5 1.00     3984     5301 30.0    OK
#>  cp_2        66.6937 23.21  17.01  98.4 1.00     3496     5260 70.0    OK
#> 
#> Population-level parameters:
#>    parameter    mean    sd  lower upper rhat ess_bulk ess_tail  sim match
#>  Intercept_1 13.9557 17.53 -19.87  47.7 1.00     9356     8910 10.0    OK
#>  time_2      -0.0088  0.63  -1.24   1.2 1.00     9087     8988  0.5    OK
#>  Intercept_3 13.5636 17.41 -20.94  47.9 1.00     8841     8553 15.0    OK
#>  time_3       0.0193  0.62  -1.22   1.2 1.00     9023     8947 -0.3    OK
#>  sigma_1      6.3353  7.29   0.19  25.0 1.00     8599     8635  3.5    OK
plot(demo_fit, prior = TRUE)


# Show all priors. Default priors are added where you don't provide any
prior_summary(demo_fit)
#> # A tibble: 7 × 5
#>   parameter   segment dpar  prior                                        bounds 
#>   <chr>         <int> <chr> <chr>                                        <chr>  
#> 1 cp_1              2 NA    uniform(min = 0.61863, max = 99.741)         [0.618…
#> 2 cp_2              3 NA    uniform(min = 0.61863, max = 99.741)         [0.618…
#> 3 Intercept_1       1 mu    normal(mean = 13.825, sd = 17.383)           none   
#> 4 time_2            2 mu    normal(mean = 0, sd = 0.62124)               none   
#> 5 Intercept_3       3 mu    normal(mean = 13.825, sd = 17.383)           none   
#> 6 time_3            3 mu    normal(mean = 0, sd = 0.62124)               none   
#> 7 sigma_1           1 sigma student_t(df = 3, location = 0, scale = 5.7) [0, In…

# Set priors and re-run
prior = list(
  Intercept_1 = 15,
  time_2 = "dt(0, 2, 1) T(0, )",  # t-dist slope. Truncated to positive.
  cp_2 = "dunif(min(time), 80)"   # change point to segment 3 before 80 (and after cp_1).
)

fit3 = mcp(model, data = data, prior = prior, seed = 42)

# Reuse coefficients in later segments using same() (e.g., Intercept_1 in segment 3)
model_same = list(
  response ~ 1,
  ~ 0 + time,
  ~ same(1, as = 1) + time  # Reuse Intercept_1 instead of estimating Intercept_3
)
fit_same = mcp(model_same, data = data, sample = FALSE)

# Show the JAGS model
demo_fit$jags_code
#> model {
#>   # Change points
#>   cp_0 = min(time)
#>   cp_1 ~ dunif(cp_0, cp_3)  # Flat Dirichlet on the segment lengths
#>   cp_2 ~ dunif(cp_0, cp_3)  # Flat Dirichlet on the segment lengths
#>   cp_3 = max(time)
#>   cp_order_ ~ dbern(step(cp_2 - cp_1))  # Ordered change points
#> 
#>   # Priors for population-level effects
#>   Intercept_1 ~ dnorm(13.825120048974153, 1/(17.382500430759464)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default)
#>   time_2_end_ ~ dnorm(Intercept_1, 1/(0.62123709509255609*(cp_2-cp_1))^2)   # Autoscaled mean coefficient (rstanarm default); sampled as the value at the segment end
#>   time_2 = (time_2_end_ - (Intercept_1)) / (cp_2 - cp_1)
#>   Intercept_3_end_ ~ dnorm(13.825120048974153 + time_3 * (cp_3 - cp_2), 1/(17.382500430759464)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default); sampled as the value at the segment end
#>   Intercept_3 = Intercept_3_end_ - (time_3 * (cp_3 - cp_2))
#>   time_3 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(0.62123709509255609)^2)   # Autoscaled mean coefficient (rstanarm default)
#>   sigma_1 ~ dt(0, 1/(5.7)^2, 3) T(0,)  # Positive residual SD calibrated on the response scale
#> 
#>   # Model and likelihood
#>   for (i_ in 1:length(time)) {
#>     # par_x local to each segment
#>     x_local_1_[i_] = min(time[i_], cp_1)
#>     x_local_2_[i_] = min(time[i_], cp_2) - cp_1
#>     x_local_3_[i_] = min(time[i_], cp_3) - cp_2
#>     
#>     # Formula for mu
#>     link_mu_[i_] =
#>       (time[i_] >= cp_0) * (time[i_] < cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(1)], c(Intercept_1)) * 1 + 
#>       (time[i_] >= cp_1) * (time[i_] < cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(2)], c(time_2)) * x_local_2_[i_] + 
#>       (time[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(3)], c(Intercept_3)) * 1 + 
#>       (time[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(4)], c(time_3)) * x_local_3_[i_]
#>     
#>     # Formula for sigma
#>     link_sigma_[i_] =
#>       (time[i_] >= cp_0) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(5)], c(sigma_1)) * 1
#> 
#>     # Likelihood for family = gaussian()
#>     mu_[i_] = link_mu_[i_]
#>     sigma_[i_] = max(1e-05, link_sigma_[i_])
#>     response[i_] ~ dnorm(mu_[i_], 1 / sigma_[i_]^2)
#>   }
#> }
# }
